wachiman.text:
canManage() gives realm-wide group manage to holders of a VIEW-only all-groups permission

`canManage()` returns `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so an all-groups permission that grants only `view` makes it return true. `GroupsResource.java:181` gates top-level group creation and moves with `auth.groups().requireManage()`. A V2 admin who was given only view on all groups can therefore create and re-parent top-level groups. The interface javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator.java:73-77) repeats this behaviour. `testManageAllGroups` only grants MANAGE, so the tests don't catch it. Fix: check only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE` here, and add a test where a VIEW-only all-groups permission gets 403 on group creation.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs, not group IDs, and never finds per-group resources

`findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` only matches resources whose type is `Groups`. Only the all-groups resource gets that type (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:274). Per-group resources are created by name only, with no type set (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:121). The loop then passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission`, which looks it up by name and falls back to the type resource. It adds the *resource* ID to `granted`, where ClientPermissionsV2.java:140 adds `resource.getName()`.

What this breaks:
- A per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grant is never returned, so `UsersResource.getUsersCount` (UsersResource.java:398/425/430) returns a count from an empty group set, while the list endpoint shows the user through per-user `canView`. The count disagrees with the list and nothing reports an error.
- With an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS grant, the set holds the type-resource ID. `searchForUser` (UsersResource.java:448-451, BruteForceUsersResource.java:147-150) puts that ID in `UserModel.GROUPS`, which filters the search to members of a group that doesn't exist, so the list comes back empty.

Fix: collect the IDs of groups that are actually granted (resource name = group id), and handle the all-groups grant separately, for example by returning empty and letting per-user evaluation decide.

Does group deletion break when both ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and _V2 are enabled?

The listener is registered when V1 is enabled. `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` when V2 is enabled (lines 66-70), so a GroupRemovedEvent now reaches `GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled`, which throws UnsupportedOperationException (GroupPermissionsV2.java:173-175). Deleting a group would then fail. Can the two features be enabled together? If so, the listener should skip V2.

requireManageMembers javadoc names the wrong method

The javadoc says it throws when `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` is false, but GroupPermissions.java:376-379 checks `canManageMembers(group)`.

Group-member visibility tests don't check users/count

These tests pass because `toRepresentation` evaluates `canView` per user. They never call `users().count()`, which depends on `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` and is wrong for V2 (see the finding on GroupPermissionsV2.java:121). Asserting the count would catch that.

Two providers with the same order no longer fail; one is picked silently by classpath order

The old `foundProviders.size() > 1` check threw `IllegalStateException`, so a deployment that shipped two real providers failed fast. Now every real provider returns 200: `DefaultCryptoProvider` (crypto/default/.../DefaultCryptoProvider.java:83), `FIPS1402Provider` (crypto/fips1402/.../FIPS1402Provider.java:114) and `WildFlyElytronProvider` (crypto/elytron/.../WildFlyElytronProvider.java:76). The sort is stable, so when two of them tie, whichever ServiceLoader returns first wins. That is classpath order, and the losers are only logged at debug level (line 69).

Example: a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has keycloak-crypto-default on the classpath used to refuse to start. Now it may quietly run on the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, and nothing at the default log level says so.

Fix: keep the order-based preference, but still throw (as before) when more than one provider shares the highest `order()`. The authz-client provider (order 100) can still lose to a single real provider without an error.

Round-trip test only checks the new codec against itself, on one curve for all three algorithms

The constructor makes a single key with the default size (`KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, line 42). That one key is then used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so at least two of the three tests sign on a curve that doesn't match the algorithm's `getSignatureLength()`.

The assertion only compares `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` with itself after a trip through `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`. If `integerToBytes` truncated r/s, or the encoder produced bad DER, both calls would be wrong in the same way and the test would still pass.

To actually test the codec:
- generate a key on the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1/384r1/521r1);
- check that `asn1Des` passes `Signature.verify` with the public key;
- check that the concatenated length equals `getSignatureLength()`.

Dead encoder calls

Lines 114-115 build two `ASN1Encoder` instances and throw away the results. The real encoding is done at lines 117-121. These two lines can be removed.

New abstract `order()` breaks external CryptoProvider implementations

`CryptoProvider` is a public SPI loaded through ServiceLoader. Adding an abstract method means any implementation outside this repository stops compiling, or throws `AbstractMethodError` at line 57 when sorted. All in-repo implementations were updated. Should this be a `default` method instead, with a documented default value, so third-party providers keep working?

The reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can run before its last request finishes

The test sets `deletedAll` and then checks `caughtExceptions` right away. The reader thread started at line 139 is never joined. A `groups()` call that is still running when the last delete returns can fail after the assertion at line 157 has already passed. That request overlaps the final deletions, which makes it one of the likeliest to hit the race. The thread also keeps running past the end of the test method. Keep a reference to the `Thread` and call `join()` (with a timeout) after `deletedAll.set(true)` and before the assertion. Also, the test only fails when the race happens to occur, so it does not reliably reproduce the bug it guards against.

The three paged `getSubGroupsStream` overloads still dereference a null delegate

`getSubGroupsCount` now handles `modelSupplier.get()` returning null when the group was deleted concurrently. The three paged `getSubGroupsStream` overloads at lines 256, 262 and 268 call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` without that check, so the same concurrent delete still ends in an NPE there. These overloads back subgroup listing, for example `GroupResource` at services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/GroupResource.java:191. Consider applying the same guard, returning `Stream.empty()`, so the fix covers the whole race and not just the count.

Hierarchy population can still NPE if a parent group is deleted concurrently

In the same request path, `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` returns null if the parent was removed after the child was loaded. `parentModel` then goes into `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)`, `toRepresentation(..., parentModel, ...)` and `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, ...)` with no null check. This is the concurrent read/delete scenario the PR targets, but one level up. A null check that drops the orphaned child would close it.

Typo in `groupUuuids`, whitespace-only line 117, empty line in the catch block

The variable `groupUuuids` has an extra `u`. Line 117 contains only whitespace, and the catch block at lines 145-146 starts with a stray empty line.

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` is called with no arguments, and no such method exists

The only declaration is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` at `UsernamePasswordForm.java:160`. A search of the repository finds no overload without arguments in `UsernamePasswordForm`, `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` or anywhere else, so the `services` module will not compile. The call should be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. Even with that fixed, a user who is already set and has no passkey credential would now be shown a username form with the username field hidden (`UsernamePasswordForm.java:100`) when they used to skip straight past it, unless the predicate also checks that the user actually has a passkey (see the finding on `UsernamePasswordForm.java:161`).

The `user != null` check turns passkeys off for normal (unidentified) login

Before this change, `fillContextForm` ran only when no user was selected: it sat inside the `else` (user == null) branch of `authenticate`, and `challenge` checked `context.getUser() == null`. The new predicate requires `user != null`. So on a first login (`authenticate` line 115, and the error re-render in `challenge` line 137), the conditional-UI and webauthn form data are never set up. Passkeys stay available only during re-authentication, and they disappear from the plain login page. The PR's own tests expect the opposite: `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.java:196` and `:238` assert that `//form[@id='webauth']` is present on the initial `oauth.openLoginForm()`, where no user is set yet. The likely intent is `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`. That keeps passkeys on the first login, offers them on re-authentication, and hides them for an identified user who has no passkey.

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` disables passkeys for the whole realm, so it never tests a user without a passkey

The comments (lines 277 and 304) say passkeys should be hidden on re-authentication because this user has no passkey. But the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, so `isPasskeysEnabled()` is false and the button is hidden for every user. The case that matters is still untested: passkeys enabled in the realm, re-authentication with `prompt=login`, and a user who has only a password. With the current predicate (`UsernamePasswordForm.java:161`) that user would be shown the passkey form, because the predicate only checks `user != null`. Consider running this scenario with passkeys enabled. Also, the try/`fail`/catch(Exception) pattern at lines 291-296 and 312-317 could be replaced with `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)`, which the organization test already uses.

Hung flusher processes are never killed, so a restart runs two flushers on the same shards

In production, processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds `SpawnProcess` objects. In CPython, `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`, a sibling class). So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False here, and `process.kill()` never runs. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally.

When `cause == "hang"` (for example, a stall on Redis or on `future.result()`), `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second process for the same shards. That second process gets the same `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values (lines 116-117), while the stuck one keeps running. Once the stuck one recovers, both processes flush the same queue keys at the same time, and segments are produced twice to buffered-segments before `done_flush_segments` removes them. The old process also keeps writing `healthy_since`, which hides later hangs. Each hang leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS.

Fix: check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or check `hasattr`-free against `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which matches the type annotation at line 68. `join` (line 346) has the same check, so `terminate()` is never called there either. That part is pre-existing. Also, the new `break` at line 341 skips the terminate for every remaining process once the deadline passes.

Per-process buffers multiply the `max-flush-segments` budget and loosen the backpressure threshold

`SpansBuffer.flush_segments` computes `max_segments_per_shard = ceil(max_flush_segments / len(self.assigned_shards))` (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:382-384). It sets `any_shard_at_limit` when a segment has `>= max_segments_per_shard` entries (buffer.py:411-412).

Before this change, one buffer held all N shards, so each flush cycle was capped at `max-flush-segments` in total. Now each of the P processes owns a buffer with N/P shards. Each process may flush up to `max-flush-segments` per cycle, so the consumer as a whole can flush up to P times that, and the per-shard limit rises from M/N to M·P/N. The backpressure trigger at flusher.py:172 therefore fires later than the option intends.

An operator who sets `--flusher-processes` silently changes what `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` means. Either divide the option by `num_processes` or document the new meaning.

Redis memory info is fetched once per flusher buffer on every submit

Every `SpansBuffer` gets the same client from `get_redis_client()` (buffer.py:162-163), and `get_memory_info` calls `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)` (buffer.py:375-376). Looping over `self.buffers` therefore sends the same INFO requests P times on each `submit`, and the ratio comes out the same. One call is enough. The same applies to `record_stored_segments` at line 269-270, although there each buffer at least covers different shards.

`time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing because the test patched `time.sleep` to a no-op

Line 15 runs `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the call at line 62 returns immediately and gives the flusher thread no time, despite the comment. The test only passes because `step.join()` with no timeout busy-waits until the thread exits. Remove the sleep and comment, or use a non-patched sleep as `test_flusher.py` does.

The multi-process restart and health-check path has no test

`test_flusher_processes_limit` only checks counts in the shard map. Nothing tests `_ensure_processes_alive` restarting one process out of several, or that flushing works when shards are split across processes. A restart test with real spawn processes would have caught the `isinstance` bug at flusher.py:254.

Docstring says the flusher creates one process per shard, but the count is capped

The number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(shards))`, and the CLI default is 1 (consumers/__init__.py:434). With the default, all shards share one process.

`_create_process_for_shard` has no callers, and the `if not process` guard is dead code

Nothing calls `_create_process_for_shard`. At line 222, `if not process: continue` can never skip, because Process and Thread objects are always truthy and the dict only ever holds started processes.

Metric tag key is `shards` here but `shard` everywhere else

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards`, while `produce` and `segment_size_bytes` (lines 185, 195) use `shard`. Values also differ: those carry the comma-joined list, and `flusher_unhealthy` (line 244) carries a single int. Dashboards can't group these metrics consistently.

Error IDs zipped against nodestore values by position, but get_multi does not keep input order

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns one value per input ID, in input order. It doesn't. `get_multi` (src/sentry/nodestore/base.py:184) removes duplicate IDs, and it builds the result from the uncached IDs first, then adds the cached ones with `items.update(cache_items)` (base.py:199-205). It also drops IDs that aren't found, because `_get_bytes_multi` only returns hits. So when some events are cached, some are missing, or the replay's `error_ids` has duplicates, each error ID gets paired with a different event's title, message and timestamp. Seer then gets wrong error context and nothing reports it. Look each one up by key instead: `data = events.get(node_id)` for each `(event_id, node_id)` pair.

Error timestamps (seconds) compared with replay event timestamps (likely milliseconds)

The merge compares `error_events[i]["timestamp"]`, the error event's `timestamp` from nodestore, against `event.get("timestamp", 0)` from the rrweb recording segments. Error event timestamps are float seconds since the epoch. rrweb event timestamps are milliseconds. If that holds here, every error timestamp is smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb, not interleaved in time order. The log lines would also show two different timestamp scales. Please confirm the units and convert one side (for example `timestamp * 1000` for errors) before comparing.

Assemble analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` check, so requests that then get a 403/404 are also counted as assembles. Moving the record after the feature gate (or after validation) would count only real assemble requests.

age/timestamp exclusivity uses truthiness, so 0 and a missing field both slip through

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check `self.initial_data.get(...)` for truthiness. A report with `age: 0` plus a `timestamp` (or `timestamp: 0` plus an `age`) passes even though both fields are present. A report with neither field also passes, because both are `required=False`. If the goal is exactly one of the two, check `"age" in self.initial_data` inside a `validate()` method.

`Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true

`normalizeDateTimeParams` returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always `true`. The query is effectively gated only by the feature flag. Drop the check, or test the specific fields it was meant to guard.

get_environment_info makes one recommended-event lookup per issue

Both the GitHub and GitLab merged-PR comment builders call `get_environment_info(issue)` for every issue in the list. Each call runs `issue.get_recommended_event()`, which queries the event store, so a comment with N issues makes N sequential event-store queries inside the comment task. The issue list is small, but these calls add up with no overall time limit.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is typed

The `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` check sits inside the `.filter` that only runs after the early return at line 61 (`if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;`). So with an empty search box, which is the default state, `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` still show up. They only disappear once the user types something. Apply the hidden filter to `sorted` before the early return, e.g. `const sorted = sortAttributes(attributes).filter(a => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(a.name));`.

Flex replacements drop align-items/gap the old styled components had

The removed `Container` was `styled(FlexBox)`, so it had `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)` as well as `justify-content: space-between`. The new `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` (line 93) sets only `justify`. The second placeholder group (line 27, `<Flex>`) also loses the `align-items: center` and `gap` that `FlexBox` gave it. Unless the vitals and tabs are meant to realign, add `align="center" gap={space(1)}` to keep the layout the same.

Removed FlexBox set height: 100%, which the Flex replacement does not

The deleted `FlexBox` had `height: 100%` as well as `flex-grow: 1; flex-direction: column`. `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` keeps only the grow and direction. When the parent is not a flex container (or its height comes from a percentage), the waterfall may no longer fill its container. Please check the trace view layout, or keep `height: 100%`.

Query options retry:false / staleTime:0 / refetchOnWindowFocus:false dropped, and environment no longer sent

The old `useApiQuery` call set `staleTime: 0`, `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` and `retry: false`, and sent `environment: selection.environments`. The new `useQuery` call uses the client defaults and leaves out environment (the comment in useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys says it is unsupported). Was this intended? If the defaults allow retries, a failing attributes endpoint now retries before `error` is set. `isLoading` now also follows `isFetching`, so background refetches report loading too.

Typo "the the" in story text

"Below is the the most basic example" should read "Below is the most basic example".

No test posts with the browser's application/reports+json content type anymore

Before this change, `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and `test_handles_multiple_reports` posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. The rewritten `test_basic`, `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs` and the new validation tests drop that argument, so they use the test client's default JSON format. Browsers send `application/reports+json`. The endpoint handles that type with the custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` (`src/sentry/issues/endpoints/browser_reporting_collector.py:69`, `:82`), and after this change no test exercises that parser. If the parser or its registration breaks, the suite stays green. Keeping `content_type="application/reports+json"` in at least `test_basic` would cover the real ingestion path.

"Project not found" may flash while the projects store is still loading

`useProjectFromId` looks the id up in `useProjects().projects` and returns `undefined` when there is no match (`static/app/utils/useProjectFromId.tsx:8-10`). It does not tell "not loaded yet" apart from "does not exist". The new branch shows an error Alert whenever `replayRecord.project_id` is set and the project is not in the store. If the replay details page can render before the org's projects are in the store, users would briefly see a false error instead of the loading spinner. Could this branch also check `useProjects().fetching` (or whether the store is initially loaded) before showing the error?

Breadcrumb timestamps are in seconds here, but real rrweb events use milliseconds, which hides a unit mismatch in error interleaving

The new tests set the top-level rrweb event `timestamp` to `now.timestamp()`, which is in seconds (here at line 188 and at 254; `test_get_request_data` uses 1.5/2.0 at 290/298). Real recording events carry milliseconds at that key. The repository's own fixtures show it: `tests/sentry/replays/unit/test_event_parser.py:329` uses `"timestamp": 1674291701348`, and the seconds value sits in `data.payload.timestamp` (line 333). `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[i]["timestamp"]` (the event timestamp from nodestore, in seconds, read at `src/sentry/replays/endpoints/project_replay_summarize_breadcrumbs.py:115`) against `event.get("timestamp", 0)` (line 155). With real data, every error timestamp (~1.7e9) is smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp (~1.7e12). So all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb, and the chronological interleaving these tests claim to check never happens in production. The log lines also mix units: `as_log_message` prints ms, the error line prints seconds. Nothing reports this, and Seer gets a misleading timeline. Use millisecond timestamps for breadcrumbs in these fixtures, matching real recordings. The interleaving assertion in `test_get_request_data` will then fail until the endpoint converts one side, e.g. compares against `error_timestamp * 1000`.

Renamed class `...TopNEventsSpans` doesn't store spans

`OrganizationEventsStatsTopNEventsSpans` stores error events built from messages and fingerprints, plus one `load_data("transaction")` event, through the discover/events path (lines 1264-1339). It stores no spans. The new name suggests it covers the spans dataset, and the new `OrganizationEventsStatsTopNEventsLogs` comment (line 3087, "implemented almost exactly the same as spans") relies on that reading. Consider a name that matches what it covers, e.g. keep `OrganizationEventsStatsTopNEvents` or use `...Discover`.

OptimizedCursorPaginator treats the datetime key as a number, so every optimized audit-log request returns 500

The endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py:80), so `self.key` is `datetime` (paginator.py:64-65). `get_item_key` copies `Paginator.get_item_key` (paginator.py:222-224) and calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a `datetime`, which raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])` whenever the page has rows and no cursor value (cursors.py:121-122, 137, 197), so any admin request with `optimized_pagination=true` against a non-empty log fails with a 500.

`value_from_cursor` (line 843) also returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `datetime <= <int>` (paginator.py:119-126), which compares a timestamp column with an integer. `DateTimePaginator` (paginator.py:233-241) does the conversion in both directions. Fix: subclass `DateTimePaginator` (or reuse its `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor`) instead of copying the integer `Paginator` logic, and add a test that runs the optimized path on real audit-log rows.

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is read on every request and crashes when there is no member

`RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` (organizations/services/organization/model.py:346). Line 71 runs on every request, including ones that never ask for `optimized_pagination`. Whenever the caller is not `request.user.is_superuser` and has no membership row, it raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns 500 where it used to return the audit log. Callers with no membership row include API-key/token auth, which has no member, and a caller let in by `OrganizationAuditPermission` through `is_active_superuser` (organization.py:124) without the `is_superuser` flag being the short-circuit. Fix: only compute this when `use_optimized` is true, and guard it, e.g. `member is not None and member.has_global_access`.

The negative-offset branch cannot work: Django querysets reject negative slicing

The comment says "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically". It does not: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for a negative start. `paginate` only turns `BadPaginationError` into a 400 (base.py:540-541), so a cursor such as `0:-5:0` sent by an admin with `optimized_pagination=true` produces an unhandled 500. The branch is also described as giving "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Pagination should never be able to do that, and it relies on "permissions are checked at the queryset level". Remove the branch and reject negative offsets with `BadPaginationError` so the client gets a 400.

The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser` and `has_global_access`, which don't match "authorized administrators"

Elsewhere this permission layer checks superuser with `is_active_superuser(request)` (organization.py:70, 124). `request.user.is_superuser` is only the raw user flag and ignores whether the superuser session is active. `has_global_access` means the member can reach every team, for example through open membership; it is not an admin role. If the optimized paginator is kept, gate it the same way as the rest of the endpoint, or drop the gate, since audit-log access is already enforced by `OrganizationAuditPermission`.

The BasePaginator comment says negative offsets are safe, but prev cursors with a negative offset still crash

Line 182 clamps only non-prev offsets to 0. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset still goes into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and Django raises `ValueError` for that. The comment "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is false. `BasePaginator.get_result` is shared by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator` and every subclass used across the API. Clamping both directions (or rejecting negative offsets with `BadPaginationError`) would match what the comment claims.

This comment describes a change that was never made

`self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged, and `Cursor.from_string` accepted negative offsets before this PR too (cursors.py:59). The added comment suggests negative offsets are an intended, supported feature, but every queryset-backed paginator fails on them (see the paginator findings). Remove the comment.

`get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`

Apart from the negative-offset branch, lines 845-911 repeat `BasePaginator.get_result` (paginator.py:136-215) line for line, including the `else` branch at 884-886, which is the same as the new base code at 182-184. Once the negative-offset branch goes, the subclass adds nothing, and the copy will drift from fixes made to the base.

The new pagination path and the changed paginator have no tests

The PR adds a paginator and a request flag, and changes offset handling in `BasePaginator`, but it adds no tests. A single endpoint test with `optimized_pagination=true` and one audit-log row would have caught the `TypeError` in `get_item_key`. A request with no membership (API key) would have caught the `member` dereference.

TotalDocs reads the cache map with no lock while BuildIndex writes to it

`TotalDocs` loops over `b.cache` (line 146) without taking `cacheMu`. Line 138 now writes the map under `cacheMu.Lock()`, but a lock only one side takes does not stop the race. This PR adds a new caller, `search.go:216`, and it runs right after `search.go:207` has started the `handleEvent` goroutine. `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex` can then write `b.cache[key]` while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. The Prometheus collector does the same thing on every scrape (`bleve_index_metrics.go:96`). Go stops the whole process with `concurrent map iteration and map write` when this happens. Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`/`RUnlock()` in `TotalDocs`.

Init workers share one `err` variable (and `totalBatchesIndexed`), and now really run in parallel

Each `group.Go` closure assigns the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns it. `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) is also shared. Before this PR, `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole build, so builds ran one at a time. With the lock moved to just the map write (bleve.go:137-139), `initWorkers` builds now overlap. The only trace is an exception log line per message.

The StreamProcessor's commit path stages and commits offsets on the same consumer object the main thread is polling. Two problems follow: the calls race with `poll`, and a commit can land during or after a revocation for partitions this consumer no longer owns. Any error is only logged (:290-291). `close()` sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread (:336-337), and only then shuts down the pool (:338). Any item a worker finishes after that point never gets its offset committed. On top of that, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` first (:233-234). The `while not self.shutdown` check at :129 makes each worker leave after its current item, so `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` never gets to drain the queue. Whatever is still queued at close is abandoned and redelivered to the next owner. Results that were processed but not committed get processed a second time. Each shutdown joins every worker one after another with `timeout=5.0` (:242-243), on top of the 5 s commit-thread join (:337). With the default 20 queues and stuck workers, one revocation can block for over 200 s. That can exceed `max.poll.interval.ms` and trigger another rebalance. Before this change, `getUserPermissions` served the scope map from `permCache` for 30s, whatever the Check outcome. OAuth `state` is the pipeline signature, a public constant, so it gives no CSRF protection

Login cache is not invalidated when an IDP in a disabled organization is updated

`update()` reads `original` through `this.getById` (line 91). When the ORGANIZATION feature is on, that returns the org-aware wrapper, and its `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled (lines 434-444). The cached ID set, though, comes from `idpDelegate.getForLogin`, and the JPA query only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` column (JPAIdentityProviderStorageProvider.java:234-238). Or make the invalidation decision with the same per-IDP fields the JPA query uses (enabled, linkOnly, hideOnLogin, organizationId, BROKER_PUBLIC), not the org-aware `isEnabled()`. The new test never disables the organization, so it does not cover this case.

Cleanup removes the literal alias "alias", not the created IDPs

`testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove` registers a removal of an IDP named `alias`, which does not exist. Outside Dev mode, every request that reads a nil cache at line 42 (all concurrent requests at cold start, or every request after a load failure) waits on `Lock()` at line 48 and then rebuilds the manifest itself. Debug logging left in at Error level, including full ID lists, on every batch

Every batch in `CleanAnnotations` (534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (576, 579) calls `r.log.Error`, even when nothing went wrong and `count` is 0. `untilDoneOrCancelled` (643-661) always runs at least one batch, and each annotation type does a MaxAge and a MaxCount pass, so every cleanup cycle logs at least one Error line per pass plus one for tags, and `cleanup.go:77` now runs a cycle every minute. This ticker drives the whole `clean` run (96-105): temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs and query history. So this one-line change runs all of these jobs ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. The 9-minute timeout at line 89 was sized for a 10-minute interval. Inline ID list is built in quadratic time

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole growing string on every iteration. This branch only runs when the batch size is above 999, so it handles large batches: with a batch of 32767 IDs it copies a few GB per batch, and does so in each loop of `untilDoneOrCancelled`. "running the max count delete again" no longer runs the delete again

Each subtest now creates its own data (116) and wipes `annotation` and `annotation_tag` in `t.Cleanup` (120-127). Background legacy writes use the request context, so they can be cancelled once the response is sent

Each of the four async legacy writes (Create here, Delete at 110, Update at 135, DeleteCollection at 163) builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the request context. The handler returns `created` right away (line 59). After that, the API server finishes the request and cancels its context. A child timeout context gets cancelled along with its parent, so any legacy SQL call still running fails with `context canceled`. That happens well before the 10s timeout. In Mode 3 the legacy store is the fallback copy, so writes are lost depending on timing, and nothing tells the user (see the next finding). Mode 1 (`dualwriter_mode1.go:54`) has the same pattern.

Failed legacy writes are no longer logged; only a metric label changes

Before this change, a failed `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` was logged ("unable to create object in legacy storage", etc.). The new goroutines (lines 55-56, 112-113, 139-140, 165-166) drop the error after passing `err != nil` to a duration histogram. If the legacy store falls behind the unified store (a timeout, a conflict, or the cancellation above), nothing in the logs shows it. Rolling back from Mode 3 would then serve stale or missing data with no warning. Log the error with `log.Error(errObjectSt, "unable to create object in legacy storage")` in each goroutine, as `dualwriter_mode2.go:47` does.

Duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or with the wrong label

Four calls record the wrong thing:
- line 45: a failed `Storage.Create` is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration`.
- line 129: a failed `Storage.Update` is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration`.
- line 166: the legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `recordStorageDuration`.
- line 106: a successful delete passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This puts each object name into the label slot (`metrics.go:59-61`), creates unbounded label cardinality, and mismatches the error path at line 103.

Legacy update gets the raw objInfo instead of the object the unified store wrote

The old code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`, so legacy received the object the unified store had already written. The new code passes the caller's original `objInfo`. Legacy then runs `UpdatedObject` against its own copy, which can differ (different resourceVersion, or a patch applied to a stale base). The two stores can end up with different content, and the precondition check may reject the request. That failure is invisible (see the logging finding). Consider keeping the `updateWrapper` with `res`.

A NotFound from the unified store now skips the legacy delete

Before, `Delete` ignored `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error returns early, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy, for example one not synced before the switch to Mode 3, can no longer be deleted through this writer, and it stays in legacy. The goroutine reuses the caller's `obj` without the DeepCopy that Mode 1 does

`dualwriter_mode1.go:51-53` deep-copies the object before handing it to the background write. Here `obj` is shared with the caller and with whatever `Storage.Create` did to it, then read concurrently by `Legacy.Create` after the handler has returned. Delete attaches `d.Log` to the context instead of `log`

Every other method calls `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Here the logger with `name`/`kind`/`method` is dropped from the context that the storage and legacy calls receive.

The tests never check the legacy writes, and the names say they don't happen

Legacy and storage share a single `mock.Mock` (lines 51-54), so the same expectation matches calls from both. The async legacy goroutine is never awaited, and nothing like `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls` runs. The tests would pass if the dual write were removed entirely. In the list view, `GrafanaRuleListItem` passes only `promRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx:47), so `rule` is undefined. `canSilence` now comes out true from the promRule path (AlertRuleMenu.tsx:96), so the 'Silence notifications' item shows up (AlertRuleMenu.tsx:126-131). It will also reconcile list items by index, so when the filter results change or more results load, per-item state such as an open delete modal, the silence drawer or the clone redirect can stay attached to the wrong rule. Test treats losing Delete/Pause as expected behaviour

The test grants AlertingRuleDelete and AlertingRuleUpdate in `beforeEach` (lines 48-62), then asserts the menu has exactly 4 items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export). With delete permission granted, a correct menu would include Delete. Pause probably as well, since the fixture rule appears to be an unprovisioned alerting rule (not verified). The assertion records the regression described on AlertRuleMenu.tsx:165 rather than catching it. It also never clicks Silence to check that a drawer opens.

Every list row now runs both the ruler and prom ability hooks, twice

`RuleActionsButtons.V2` and `AlertRuleMenu` each call the ruler hook (`useRulerRuleAbility`/`useRulerRuleAbilities`) and the prom hook (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`). RTK Query dedups the network requests, but the hook work and memo churn repeat for every rule on a page this PR is meant to make lighter. Consider computing abilities once in `RuleActionsButtons` and passing them down, or skipping the ruler path when `rule` is undefined.

Templating and ad-hoc filters now run two or three times per sub-request, so parsed-label filters get duplicated

`runSplitQuery` now calls `applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters)`. Each sub-request then goes through `datasource.runQuery` → `super.query`, and `DataSourceWithBackend` calls `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again (packages/grafana-runtime/src/utils/DataSourceWithBackend.ts:185). `filters` is still on the sub-request because it is built as `{ ...request, targets }` (querySplitting.ts:174). The shard path adds a third pass: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates at shardQuerySplitting.ts:52, then hands each shard group to `runSplitQuery` (shardQuerySplitting.ts:154,163), which interpolates again. The updated test confirms this: `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single query.

`addAdHocFilters` is not idempotent for queries that have a parser. `addFilterAsLabelFilter` (modifyQuery.ts:511-541) appends ` | key=`value`` on every call, while only the stream-selector path de-duplicates (modifyQuery.ts:494). The results stay the same, but the query text grows, Query inspector shows it, and every shard and chunk request pays for it. A second `templateSrv.replace` pass also re-expands any variable value that itself contains `$name` text.

One option is to pass the un-interpolated targets on to the sub-requests and use the interpolated copy only for the decisions made here (`querySupportsSplitting`, `isLogsQuery`, `calculateStep`, shard selector). Another is to clear `filters` on sub-requests whose targets are already interpolated.

`applyTemplateVariables` strips `__auto` (and `__range*`) out of `scopedVars` so that the backend interpolates them (datasource.ts:1111-1125). In production `[$__auto]` reaches the backend unchanged. This test's `replace` mock ignores `scopedVars` and rewrites `$__auto` to `5m` anyway, so it asserts `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`, an outcome the real code never produces. Local cache entry is written before the limit check, so a rejected device gets in on its next request

`tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` (line 87) before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` (line 93). When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache key stays set. pkg/server/wire.go still registers ProvideAnonDBStore, whose new int64 parameter has no provider

`ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes `(db.DB, int64)`. `pkg/server/wire.go:374-375` still lists `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds `anonstore.AnonStore` to it. Requests without X-Grafana-Device-Id skip the device limit entirely

`TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing (lines 119-121) or the IP cannot be parsed (lines 125-128). `Authenticate` then grants anonymous access with no limit check. The device ID is also chosen by the client, so any client can reuse an ID that is already registered. Is `device_limit` meant only as a usage counter for the UI, or as an access limit? If it is an access limit, a request without the header should probably be refused once the limit is reached.

Separate count and insert let concurrent new devices go over the limit

`CountDevices` (line 110) and the upsert (lines 149-153) run in separate sessions with no lock or transaction. Several new devices arriving at once, or several Grafana instances in HA, can all read `count < limit` and all insert. The limit is then exceeded. If the limit must be exact, run the count and insert in one transaction, or use a conditional `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?`.

Device tagging moved from a goroutine onto the request path, using the request context

The upsert used to run in a goroutine with its own 2-minute `context.Background()` timeout. With `device_limit` set, it now runs synchronously on the request path, together with a `COUNT(*)` over `anon_device`, on every local-cache miss. This applies even when no limit is configured. The write also uses the request `ctx`. If the client disconnects, the write is cancelled, but the cache key was already set (impl.go:87), so that device is not tagged for the next 29 minutes. Consider keeping the async path when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0`.

Limit test does not cover a known device updating while the store is at its limit

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device is rejected. It never re-submits the first device (`32mdo31deeqwes`) after the limit is reached. That is the path `updateDevice` exists for, and it is what keeps existing users working. There is also no `TagDevice`/`Authenticate` test with a limit, which would have caught the local-cache bypass in impl.go:87.

New `device_limit` option is not documented in conf/defaults.ini or sample.ini

The other `[auth.anonymous]` keys, such as `hide_version`, are listed in `conf/defaults.ini:592` and `conf/sample.ini:581`. `device_limit` is not, so operators have no way to find it.

anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as possibly undefined, but the backend always sends a number, and the frontend never reads it

`FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is an `int64` with no `omitempty` (frontend_settings.go:195). The boot data therefore always contains a number, 0 when the option is unset, never `undefined`. With the `= undefined` initializer and no annotation, TypeScript also infers the class field's type as `undefined`. Nothing under `public/` reads the field. Consider `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`, or `= 0`, or leave the field out until a consumer exists.

Fallback chain depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the LRU translation cache key does not

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` now makes the result of `translate_no_cache` depend on `SiteSetting.default_locale`. But the cache in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:72` is keyed only on `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`, and that cache is shared by every site and thread in the process.

Example: a key is missing in the user's locale (`:es`) and `I18n.t(key)` is called with no options. On a multisite process, the first site to hit that key (say its default is `:fr`) caches the French string. Another site whose default is `:de` is then served the French string. The jobs code switches sites per thread inside one process (`app/jobs/base.rb:150-151`). The same goes for a single site: after an admin changes `default_locale`, the old fallback text keeps being served until the LRU evicts it. Nothing reports or logs this.

Fix: add `SiteSetting.default_locale` (or the joined fallback list) to the cache key `k`.

Fallback locales are only preloaded in the web request path; jobs can still show missing translations

`translate_accelerator.rb` loads locales lazily. `translate` only loads `config.locale` (line 68), and locales that are not loaded look empty to the backend. This PR calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` only in `ApplicationController#set_locale` (`app/controllers/application_controller.rb:159`).

Background jobs set `I18n.locale = SiteSetting.default_locale` (`app/jobs/base.rb:151`), and notifications then switch to the user's locale with `I18n.with_locale(user.effective_locale)` (`app/services/post_alerter.rb:138`). Neither calls `ensure_loaded!`. In a Sidekiq process where `:en` (or the site locale) has never been the active locale, a key missing in the user's locale goes through the fallback chain, finds nothing in the unloaded locales, and still ends up as 'translation missing'. Opening the route inside the app shows the 'stopped' message without changing anything

No test covers the new unsubscribe endpoint or the per-topic link

Typo in property name `stopNotificiationsText`

Deleting the cache doesn't refetch connectedCalendars, so the old "Last updated" stays on screen

Does `updateMany` with empty `data` actually bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`?

`updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` relies on Prisma setting the `@updatedAt` field (`schema.prisma:860`) automatically. As far as I know, Prisma's engine only adds `@updatedAt` when the write args are non-empty, and treats an empty update as a no-op. If so, this line writes nothing. Also, nothing in the PR reads `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`: the UI shows `CalendarCache.updatedAt` through `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. Cache timestamp is always formatted with the "en-US" locale

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` ignores the user's locale, while the surrounding label is translated through `t()`. A user with a non-US locale sees an M/D/YY date inside a translated sentence, and day/month order is ambiguous for them. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (`i18n.language`) instead.

`sed -i ''` is BSD-only, and `ENV_FILE` depends on the current directory

On GNU sed (Linux), `sed -i '' -E ...` treats `''` as the script and fails, so the env file is never updated. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved from the caller's current directory, not the script's location. Run from the repo root, it creates or edits a `.env` outside the repository. Resolve the path from `$(dirname "$0")`, and write the file in a portable way (e.g. a temp file plus `mv`). Also, `cleanup` exits 0 on the failure paths (lines 49, 57), which hides the failure from callers.

Existing cache rows will show the migration time as "Last updated"

`DEFAULT NOW()` fills every existing `CalendarCache` row with the deploy time. Until a webhook refreshes it, the new dropdown shows that time as the cache's last update, even though the cached data may be much older. The header comment still says the column is added "without a default value", which is no longer true.

Slots inside a date override skip the busy check, so booked times show as free

When any override falls on the slot's date and the slot is inside it, `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at line 153. The fixed-host and round-robin paths spread `...schedule` / `...userSchedule` (lines 488-493, 513-518), which carry both `dateOverrides` and `busy`. So on any day with a date override, the organizer's existing bookings, calendar events and buffers are all ignored, and invitees can book times that are already taken (double booking). Instead of returning true here, fall through to the busy check.

Working-hours check drops a slot if any one range for that day doesn't contain it

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true (slot unavailable) as soon as one entry for that weekday doesn't contain the slot. `getWorkingHours` (packages/lib/availability.ts:76-111) returns several entries per weekday in two cases: the user has split hours (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17), or their hours cross UTC midnight. For example, 09:00-17:00 in America/Los_Angeles becomes 17:00-23:59 on day d plus 00:00-01:00 on day d+1. A slot at 18:00Z on Tuesday then fails the Tue 00:00-01:00 entry and is removed. Users in those situations lose most or all of their slots, with no error. The check has to ask whether no matching entry contains the slot, e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`, and it should run only when there are entries for that day.

`end` is computed from slotStartTime, not slotEndTime

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` repeats the start time, so `end > workingHour.endTime` never catches a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end. It should use `slotEndTime`.

Two Dayjs objects compared with `===` are never equal, so this branch is dead

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares two freshly created objects by reference, so it is always false. The 'unavailable all day' case (start == end) is never caught here. A slot starting exactly at the override's start/end instant is then counted as inside the override and, because of line 133, returned as available. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `.valueOf()`.

Override day is matched by UTC date, not the organizer's local date

The override start is shifted to its real UTC instant and then compared with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`, which is also UTC. Take an organizer in UTC-8 with an override on Jan 3, 09:00-17:00 local (17:00Z Jan 3 to 01:00Z Jan 4). Normal working-hour slots on Jan 2 local evening fall on UTC Jan 3, match the override day, sit outside it, and are removed. Slots on Jan 4 00:00-01:00Z, which belong to the override day, don't match and go through the plain working-hours path. The date comparison should be done in `organizerTimeZone`.

Converted override minutes wrap at midnight, so the override is silently dropped

`.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding `offset` wraps modulo one day. If the shifted override crosses the invitee's midnight (e.g. organizer UTC-8 override 09:00-17:00 seen by a UTC invitee: start 1020, end 60), `endTime < startTime`. `buildSlots` then skips the range (`if (start >= end) continue;`, line 68), while the working hours for that user were already spliced out at lines 228-243. The invitee sees no slots that day. The active-override filter at line 207 also still selects the day using the organizer's wall-clock time stored as UTC, not the converted instant.

Parsing `Date.toString()` output and an optional `override.timeZone`

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` re-parses the engine-specific `Date.toString()` format. `dayjs(override.start)` gives the same instant without the string round-trip. `override.timeZone` is optional in `TimeRange` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts:5). When it is missing, `.tz(undefined)` falls back to the default/server zone, so the offset depends on where the code runs (this file also runs client-side, per the comment at lines 146-147).

New test doesn't cover the new checkIfIsAvailable branches

The added case only repeats the IST override scenario for a +6:00 invitee. It has no booking on the override day, so it can't catch busy times being ignored there. It has a single working-hours range per day, so it can't catch the split / UTC-midnight-straddling hours regression. A case with a booking inside the override, and one with a negative-offset organizer, would exercise the logic this PR adds.

Retry-count purge is not limited to SMS reminders

The new second `OR` branch (`retryCount > 1`) has no `method` filter, so this SMS cron deletes any `WorkflowReminder` row (EMAIL, WHATSAPP, SMS) with `retryCount > 1`, whether or not it is scheduled. This file is the only place that increments `retryCount` today, so only SMS rows are affected right now. But the column sits on the shared model (`packages/prisma/schema.prisma:1000`). If the email or WhatsApp crons start counting retries, this endpoint will quietly delete their rows, on its own 15-minute schedule. Moving `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` outside the `OR`, and adding `scheduled: false` to the retry branch, would keep the purge within its own scope. The comment at line 28 also still describes only the date-based deletion.

A failing update in the catch block now aborts the whole batch

Before this change the `catch` only logged, so one bad reminder could not stop the loop. Now it calls `prisma.workflowReminder.update`, and nothing catches an error from that call. Take a reminder that is deleted between the `findMany` at line 48 and this point, for example by `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (`packages/features/ee/workflows/lib/reminders/smsReminderManager.ts:245-251`) when a booking is cancelled or a workflow is edited. Its first update fails and jumps to this `catch`, and the update here throws P2025 as well. The handler then rejects, and every remaining reminder in `unscheduledReminders` waits until the next run 15 minutes later. Using `updateMany({ where: { id } , data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } } })`, which does not throw when no row matches, or wrapping this call in its own try/catch would keep the loop's old isolation. `{ increment: 1 }` also avoids losing a count to a stale read-then-write.

Reminders are silently deleted after two failed 15-minute runs

The cron runs every 15 minutes (`.github/workflows/cron-scheduleSMSReminders.yml:8`). Two failures in a row therefore set `retryCount` to 2, and the next run deletes the reminder, with nothing logged. Failures include a Twilio error or outage, `checkSMSRateLimit` throwing, and `scheduleSMS` returning `undefined` while the user or team is locked (`twilioProvider.ts:90-95`). So an outage of about 30 minutes, or an admin lock that is lifted later, permanently drops reminders for bookings that may be days away. Before this change they were retried until `scheduledDate`. If the cap is intended, consider logging the reminder IDs you delete, and a larger cap or a backoff, so the loss can be diagnosed.

Two branches of getBaseConditions can never run

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object. Every path of `buildAuthorizationConditions` (lines 125-143) returns either a fragment or `NOTHING_CONDITION`, never null. So `authConditions` is always truthy, and the `else if (filterConditions)` branch (line 76) and the final `NOTHING_CONDITION` branch (line 79) can never run. They also suggest that filters alone could be applied without authorization, which is not the intent. A simpler version: `return filterConditions ? Prisma.sql`(${auth}) AND (${filterConditions})` : auth;`

The constructor used to take the discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions`, so `scope: "team"` without `teamId` was a compile error. `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` makes `teamId` optional for every scope. A caller that leaves it out now compiles, fails `safeParse` at line 62, sets `options` to null, and gets `1=0`, an empty insights result with no error or log. If the looser type is needed for callers that hold a non-narrowed input, consider logging when validation fails, or keeping the union type and narrowing at the call site.

Org/team `= ANY(array)` SQL never runs against the database

The only test that runs the generated SQL (`getBaseConditions`, lines 480-484) uses `scope: "user"`. The org and team tests (lines 295-299, 332-343) only compare the `Prisma.Sql` objects structurally. So nothing checks that `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${ids})` bind correctly and return the right rows. That is exactly the part this rewrite from Prisma `in:` filters to raw SQL could break (array parameter typing, operator precedence of the OR/AND nesting). Consider adding a `$queryRaw` assertion for the org and team scopes, with one team booking and one personal booking each.

Caching tests deleted while the caching code stays

The `Caching` describe block was removed, but `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` still memoize into `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` (insightsBooking.ts:83-95). Those tests only needed their expected values changed to `Prisma.sql` form. Removing them leaves the memoization untested, including the `null`-vs-`undefined` distinction that keeps `getFilterConditions` from rebuilding when there are no filters.

Google credential key is overwritten with a SafeParse result object

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the whole `safeParse` result (`parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29`), so `key` here is `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. Line 100 writes that object to `credential.key`. The next time the service is built, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) throws, because `access_token`/`refresh_token` are now nested under `data`. This runs on every Google token refresh, whether or not credential sharing is enabled, so every Google Calendar user breaks after their first refresh. Use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (or keep `googleCredentialSchema.parse`).

Computed schema keys evaluate to the literal "[object Object]"

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both become the property name `"[object Object]"`. The second one overwrites the first, so the schema is really `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`. Zod's `z.object` strips unknown keys, so in sync mode every expiry field (`expiry_date`, `expires_in`, `instance_url`, ...) is dropped from `data`. For example, Office 365 merges `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credentials (office365calendar CalendarService.ts:264), so the stored expiry never moves forward and the token counts as expired on every call. Use `.passthrough()` (or `z.object({access_token: z.string()}).catchall(z.unknown())`) instead of computed keys.

Sync path returns a fetch Response, but several callers expect SDK or axios shapes

In sync mode this returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, and the callers were written for other return shapes:
- Google (`googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94`) reads `res?.data`, which is undefined on a Response, so line 95 throws.
- HubSpot (`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192-198`) treats it as a `HubspotToken` and writes the Response object into `credential.key`.
- Zoho Bigin (`zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`) and Zoho CRM read `.data.error` as if it were an axios response.

Only the fetch-based adapters (Office 365, Zoom, Webex, Lark) work with the sync endpoint. Either return parsed JSON in a shape every caller agrees on, or adapt each caller.

Credential id passed where the user id is expected

`refreshOAuthTokens` sends its third argument to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId` (refreshOAuthTokens.ts:11). Here it gets `credentialId` (`credential.id`, line 53), so the parent application gets asked for tokens for the wrong user, which can mean another user's tokens. Every other caller passes `credential.userId`. Pass `credential.userId` here too (it has to be threaded into `refreshAccessToken`).

`prisma` is used without an import

This file never imports `prisma` (imports at lines 1-20), so this line resolves to the global `prisma`. `packages/prisma/index.ts:56-59` sets `globalThis.prisma` only conditionally (the dev-only hot-reload cache). In production, every Salesforce client construction would then throw a ReferenceError after the token fetch. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

Salesforce refreshes on every construction, ignores the sync endpoint, and keeps using the stale token

Three problems with this block:
- `getClient` now calls Salesforce's token endpoint on every `SalesforceCalendarService` construction, with no expiry check.
- It doesn't go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so the sync endpoint is never used for Salesforce, yet in sync mode `parseRefreshTokenResponse` switches to the minimal schema and drops `instance_url`. - The new access token is saved to the database, but the `jsforce.Connection` at lines 101-108 is still built from the old `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url`.

Also, `response.statusText !== "OK"` is fragile: HTTP/2 responses have an empty statusText. Use `response.ok`.

Malformed body or bad ciphertext surfaces as an unhandled 500

`parse` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` (lines 57-59) all throw on bad input, and nothing catches them, so the caller gets a generic 500 with no message. The handler also accepts any HTTP method. Consider `safeParse`, returning 400 on decrypt/parse failure, and restricting to POST.

Webhook secret compared with `!==`

This endpoint can overwrite any user's credentials. The shared secret is checked with plain string inequality, which isn't constant-time. Consider `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers, and reject the request when the header is missing or is an array.

One failed SendGrid cancel stops every other cancellation in the run, and none of the rows get deleted

The whole cancel loop sits inside one `try` (53-77). If `client.request` throws for any reminder (lines 57-64), for example on a SendGrid error, a rate limit, or a batch that is already cancelled, the loop exits and the rest of the `remindersToCancel` never reach SendGrid. Those emails then go out for bookings that were cancelled or rescheduled. The only trace is a `console.log`.

The `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls pushed at 66-72 are lazy PrismaPromises, so they only run at `await Promise.all` on line 74. That line is skipped when an error is thrown, so even reminders that SendGrid already cancelled keep `cancelled: true`. The next cron run POSTs them first again. If SendGrid rejects a second cancel of the same batch, the same reminder fails on every run, and every cancelled reminder queued behind it stays blocked until its send time passes.

Fix: put the try/catch around each reminder, and delete or mark each row right after its own cancel succeeds.

Do the immediate-cancel callers stay under SendGrid's limit on cancelled batches?

As I understand it, the new design waits to cancel until 1 hour before the send (`scheduleEmailReminders.ts:43-51`) because SendGrid allows only a few batches in `cancel`/`pause` status at once. Three paths still cancel right away, once per reminder, in an un-awaited `forEach`: deleting a workflow (`workflows.tsx:212-218`), deleting a step (`workflows.tsx:519-525`), and rescheduling (`handleNewBooking.ts:966-972`). A workflow with many future bookings could pass that limit in one call. Each failed cancel only reaches `console.log` at line 234, and the row is removed by cascade, so nothing retries it and the email still goes out. Is that limit the reason for the deferral? If so, should these paths also defer, for example by setting `cancelled: true` before the cascade delete? Or is there a reason they can't?

Reminder cancellation is no longer awaited

The old code put the `workflowReminder.deleteMany` promises into `prismaPromises` and awaited them at line 497. Now `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are called fire-and-forget inside `forEach`, so the `cancelled: true` update or the row delete is never awaited by the handler. On a serverless runtime that freezes once the response is sent, an update that hasn't finished is lost. The cron then never cancels the batch, and the attendee gets a reminder for a cancelled booking. The same pattern was added in `bookings.tsx:488-494`, where the old `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)` was removed. Collecting the returned promises and awaiting them with the other Prisma work would bring back the old guarantee.

This try/catch never catches anything

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and handle their own errors (`emailReminderManager.ts:233-235`, `smsReminderManager.ts:187-189`). Inside a synchronous `forEach` their promises are dropped, so the `catch` at 973-975 can never fire and the 'Error while canceling scheduled workflow reminders' log never prints. Either await the calls (`Promise.all(...map(...))`) or remove the try/catch.

SMS row delete races the cascade delete of the workflow or step

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now ends with `prisma.workflowReminder.delete({ where: { id } })` (`smsReminderManager.ts:182-186`). On workflow delete (216) and step delete (523) it isn't awaited, and it races `workflow.deleteMany` (220) and `workflowStep.delete` (527). Both of those already remove the reminder through `onDelete: Cascade` (`schema.prisma:643`). Whichever finishes second gets 'Record to delete does not exist', which is logged as 'Error canceling reminder'. Nothing is lost, but every such delete produces a misleading error log. Await the cancellations before the cascade delete, or skip the row delete on these paths.

`Prisma` import is no longer used, and type-only imports became value imports

After this change `Prisma` (line 9) is unused, and `PrismaPromise` is only used as a type (line 342). The previous `import type` was turned into a value import, and the new list has no trailing comma after `Prisma`. Lines 901-961 are also re-indented inside a block comment. Restore `import type { PrismaPromise }`, remove `Prisma`, and revert the comment reformatting.

Team admin check uses && and so needs the user to be OWNER; admins are refused

`isTeamAdmin` already matches ADMIN or OWNER (packages/lib/server/queries/teams/index.ts:264-270). `isTeamOwner` matches only OWNER (:286-293). Joining them with `&&` makes `isTeamAdminOrOwner` true only for owners, so a team ADMIN who is not the organizer or an attendee gets FORBIDDEN, even though the variable name says admins are allowed.
